pr_title: fileio: introduce read_full_virtual_file() for reading virtual files …
pr_body:
…in sysfs, procfs

Virtual filesystems such as sysfs or procfs use kernfs, and kernfs can work
with two sorts of virtual files.

One sort uses "seq_file", and the results of the first read are buffered for
the second read. The other sort uses "raw" reads which always go direct to the
device.

In the later case, the content of the virtual file must be retrieved with a
single read otherwise subsequent read might get the new value instead of
finding EOF immediately. That's the reason why the usage of fread(3) is
prohibited in this case as it always performs a second call to read(2) looking
for EOF which is subject to the race described previously.

Fixes: #13585.

issue_context.title: reading a volatile sysfs attribute wih fread() is not safe
issue_context.body:
udev uses fread() to read a sysfs attribute.  If it doesn't get the requested number of bytes on the first read (which it won't), it reads again - and normally gets zero bytes on second read.

However some sysfs attributes can change value spontaneously.  In such cases it is possible that udev will see one value and part of another.

Specifically the "md/array_state" attribute of md RAID arrays can change from "clear" to "inactive" while the initial "add" event is happening.
If fread() reads at this time, it can see "clear\nve\n", which is unexpected.

rules/99-systemd.rules.in contains a rule that checks for ATTR{md/array_state}=="|clear|inactive".
(mdadm has a udev rules file with a similar condition).
This rule will fail when udev sees "clear\nve\n", which is fairly clearly not the intention.

To fix the reading of sysfs attributes, we need to avoid using fread(), or possibly use some other technique such as read repeatedly until two consecutive results are the same.

I suspect that means changing the read_full_file() call in sd_device_get_sysattr_value() to something else - probably a new function.
Is there any other call to read_full_file() that might need to be changed?
Any guidance as to how the new function should behave, before I start writing it?
comments:
Hi Neil,

> Is there any other call to read_full_file() that might need to be changed?

Most likely the same issue might happen when reading from /proc, see get_proc_field() for instance.

> Any guidance as to how the new function should behave, before I start writing it?

At a first glance, I would avoid using fread() in read_full_file() and adding a new flag which would specify that short read means EOF that could be used when reading from /sys or /proc.
Just by-the-way, the old udev_device_get_sysattr_value() prior to 
Commit f4ac4d1a82e2 ("libudev: device - replace by a thin wrapper around sd-device")
(in 2015) read the sysfs attribute correctly with read().
This commit changed that function to use sd_device_get_sysattr_value() which uses read_full_file which uses fread() which causes the problem.  Maybe we should just revert to the old code??
How large are your attributes that the first read done by fread is not sufficient?

@poettering That's not the issue, the problem is the fread() approach isn't considering a short read as EOF - it performs a subsequent read() looking for a 0 return for EOF.

This makes the sample non-atomic, so for cases like the mentioned RAID array changing from "clear" to "inactive", if the change coincides with the first short read of "clear\n", the second read instead of finding EOF immediately will read "ve\n", resuling in a "clear\nve\n" sample.

Attribute size is mostly irrelevant, it's just a simple race condition.  The read code for sampling these virtual filesystems has to assume the entire sample will come in a single read call for atomicity, and treat short reads as including EOF.  I suppose in situations where the read fills the buffer, the right thing to do would be enlarge the buffer and retry from the start until you get a short atomic read.
An attempt to fix this is waiting in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/13819, PTAL.

review_comments: Shouldn't there be maximum number of tries here?

The only way it would loop forever would be if the kernel constantly reports an incorrect file size (more data read than the reported file size)... I don't think it could happen in practice but maybe we could add an extra safety check.
You're right, it would have to grow. But we use stat, so it could grow just by one byte every time. So I think it's better to have some limit here.

This doesn't look right.

You're always allocating size + 1, and later in this function's normal return path the \0 is stored in that +1 of space.

Why isn't this instead just checking for ret_size before storing the size, and always going through the normal return path of ensuring there's a \0 terminator?  Don't look for an existing terminator in the stream, just always add one.

As the comment explained, if the caller doesn't want to know the number of bytes returned by this function *and* it contains NUL bytes (besides the trailing one) then there's no way for the caller to know how long the returned buf is so the returned contents is unusable.
BTW this part was taken from read_full_stream_full()

I think the comment doesn't make sense.

If the caller didn't ask for a size, and the contents contain a null byte, the contents are self null-terminated.  It's not unusable, it just contains a null byte, and that fulfills all safety requirements for a C string which is the only likely sane intention of use when no size was requested.  Why are we prohibiting reading a virtual file containing an already null-terminated string when the caller doesn't request the size?

I admit I'm not exactly focused on systemd/computer stuff at the moment, but this strikes me as broken.

IMNSHO the size should just be stored if requested, and a potentially redundant null terminator always added in the space allocated for it.  I'm all for defensive programming but this doesn't strike me as a meaningful example of it.

What am I missing?
